Business plan text:

Rollcrate
Executive Summary: Rollcrate
Problem
Every semester, millions of college students move into and out of dorms. Most of them use
whatever is cheap and available, like cardboard boxes, plastic bins, trash bags, and laundry
baskets. These options are not great. Cardboard boxes tear and get soggy, plastic bins are
bulky and hard to carry, and bags do not protect anything fragile. Students also have to carry
heavy loads across parking lots, up stairs, and through crowded hallways, which is tiring and
sometimes causes injuries. At the end of the year, many of these containers get thrown away,
which is wasteful, and then students have to buy new ones the next fall.
A second problem is storage. Many students who live far from campus or study abroad need
somewhere to keep their belongings over the summer. Storage companies and campus storage
programs charge fees that can add up to a few hundred dollars a year, and students often feel
they have no choice but to pay.
Solution
Rollcrate is a foldable storage crate with built-in wheels and a telescoping pull handle. When
it is unfolded, it is a sturdy container that holds a large amount of clothing, books, bedding,
and small electronics. When it is folded, it collapses to roughly the thickness of a textbook
so it can slide under a bed, behind a door, or into a closet. The crate is made from a durable
fabric-and-polymer material that is water resistant and designed to last for several years.
Because it is reusable, students do not need to buy new boxes each year.
We believe Rollcrate also helps students save on storage. Because the crate is easy to pack,
label, and stack, students can use cheaper options like a friend's garage or a shared unit, and
some campuses may let students keep crates in their own storage rooms at reduced cost.
Market
There are about nineteen million college students in the United States, and a large share of
them live on campus at some point. Our target is first and second year students who live in
dorms and their parents, who often pay for the supplies. We estimate that about eight million
students live in campus housing each year. If each of them spent forty dollars on a moving and
storage product, that would be a market of around three hundred twenty million dollars. We
think this is a reasonable estimate, though it is based on general assumptions rather than
detailed research. Our first goal is to reach a small portion of this market, starting with
schools near our own university and expanding to other regions.
Business Model
We plan to sell Rollcrate directly to students and parents through our website, with prices
around thirty-five to forty-five dollars per crate and discounts for bundles of two or four. We
also plan to sell through campus bookstores and through back-to-school promotions that connect
with housing offices. A second revenue idea is to sell sponsored crates to universities and
housing departments, which could give them to incoming students with a school logo on them. Our
cost to make each crate is currently about eighteen dollars on a small production run, and we
expect this to drop with larger orders. We have not yet tested all of these channels, and our
pricing may change as we learn more from customers.
Competition
The space for dorm and moving products is crowded. There are many existing options, including
plastic bins, rolling carts, collapsible crates, duffel bags with wheels, and large retail kits
sold each August by big-box stores and online marketplaces. Some of these products are cheap,
and some are well known. Our view is that none of them combines folding, wheels, and durability

in a single product that is designed specifically for the dorm move. Still, we know that larger
companies could copy our idea, and that students are often price sensitive and may just choose
the cheapest thing available. Our advantage is that we are focused on one customer and can move
quickly, but we do not yet have a patent or strong brand.
Team
Marcus Delacroix-Ibarra is our CEO and handles overall strategy, customer conversations, and
sales. He is a junior studying business and has experience working in a campus retail job.
Priya Venkataraghavan leads product design and is a mechanical engineering student who built
the first prototypes and manages relationships with our manufacturing contact. Tobias
Ellingsworth is responsible for marketing and our website, and has experience running social
media for a student club. Naomi Achterberg manages finances and operations, including our LLC
paperwork and order tracking. We all attend our university and work on Rollcrate part time
alongside classes.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core concept, registered Rollcrate as an LLC, built a working
prototype, and launched a website. We gave early versions of the crate to a small number of
students who tried them during a move-in weekend and gave us feedback, which was mostly
positive, although some said the handle felt loose. We have also received our first payment
from a customer, who purchased a set of crates through our website. Revenue to date is small,
under a few hundred dollars. Our spending so far has come from the founders' own savings and a
small amount of money from family, totaling about four thousand dollars, mostly for prototypes,
the website, and legal filing fees.
Over the next twelve months, we plan to complete a first production run of about five hundred
crates, improve the handle design, and sell mainly during the fall move-in season. We project
revenue of roughly fifteen to twenty thousand dollars in the first year if sales go as planned,
but this is a rough estimate and depends on how well our marketing works. We expect to be near
break-even after the first production run and to need additional funds to grow beyond that.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition to win funding and to gain mentorship. We are hoping for a
prize of around ten thousand dollars, which we would use mainly to pay for our first production
run and to improve the product based on feedback. Beyond funding, we would value guidance from
judges and advisors on pricing, how to approach university housing offices, and how to protect
our design. We would also like introductions to manufacturers and to anyone with experience
selling consumer products to students. We believe Rollcrate can make moving easier and cheaper
for students, and we are excited to keep building it.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.

response.text:
**Viability and Scalability of the Business Model and Strategy:**

**1. Viability:**
Rollcrate presents a viable business model that addresses a clear, recurring need among college students. The problem of inefficient, temporary, and wasteful dorm move and storage solutions is well-defined and widespread. The product concept—foldable, durable, and mobile storage—offers a differentiated solution that combines multiple useful features (folding, wheels, durability) into a single product tailored for dorm environments.

The business model is straightforward: direct-to-consumer sales through an online platform, campus bookstores, and back-to-school promotions, supplemented by sponsored university partnerships. The pricing model is reasonable, with a $35–$45 price point per crate, which is within the range of similar products and potentially attractive to price-sensitive students.

**2. Scalability:**
The business model has scalability potential, especially given the large and recurring market of 19 million U.S. college students. However, the current strategy is limited to a narrow geographic and demographic focus (first- and second-year students in dorms), which may restrict early growth. The estimated market size of $320 million is based on general assumptions rather than detailed research, which weakens the confidence in the scalability of the business.

**3. Path to Making Money:**
The company has a clear path to generating revenue through direct sales and university partnerships. The initial revenue from a few hundred dollars is modest, but the projected $15,000–$20,000 in Year 1 revenue is achievable if marketing and distribution channels are effectively executed. However, the estimate is speculative and depends heavily on the success of early marketing efforts and product adoption.

**4. Validity of Assumptions:**
The assumptions underlying the business model are not fully validated. The market size estimate lacks data support, and the pricing strategy has not been tested with real customers. The team has not conducted customer research or competitive analysis beyond identifying existing products, which limits the depth of their understanding of the market.

**5. Risks and Weaknesses:**
- **Competition:** The market is crowded with established products, some of which are cheaper and more widely known. Rollcrate’s differentiation is not fully substantiated, and there is a risk of being copied or outcompeted.
- **Lack of IP Protection:** The absence of a patent or strong brand increases the risk of imitation and limits long-term competitive advantage.
- **Financial Constraints:** The current funding is limited to personal savings and small family contributions, which may not be sufficient for scaling production or marketing.
- **Product Development:** The prototype has been tested with a small group, but there are still design issues (e.g., loose handle), which need to be resolved before mass production.

**Conclusion:**
Rollcrate has a viable and potentially scalable business model that addresses a real problem. However, the assumptions about market size, pricing, and competition are not sufficiently validated. The company needs to conduct more rigorous market research, test its pricing strategy with real customers, and secure IP protection to strengthen its position. With the right execution and additional funding, Rollcrate could grow into a meaningful player in the dorm storage market.
